# Annotation algorithms

There are two possible approaches of doing cell type annotation: using suppervised or unsupervised methods. Of course there are many different libraries that offer many different algorithms for both methods but, for the sake of simplicity, we will only consider the ones offered by the libraries used in the QC exploration, Seurat and SingleExperiment but now we will also consider Single R.

It's important to mention that according to our data we should not do supervised methods ortherwise it will introduce huge bias. In other words, if you do not have a reference made specifically for your sample and protocol you should not use a reference; it is really important that age, sex, tissue, biologucal surroundings, etc are the same in oth sample and reference. So **supervised methods here will only be for academical purposes and not executed**. With the exception of SingleR algorithm which performs unbiased identification of cell types in single cell transcriptomics data based on built-in
reference transcriptomes of pure cell types.                                 

## Unsupervised

#### Spatial Experiment object
If it is a `Spatial Experiment` object you can have this unsupervised algorithm:
```r
library(scran)
# shared nearest-neighbor (SNN) graph based on 
# cell-to-cell Jaccard similarity in PC space
g <- buildSNNGraph(pvp, use.dimred="PCA", type="jaccard", BPPARAM=bp)
# community detection using Leiden algorithm
k <- cluster_leiden(g, objective_function="modularity", resolution=0.7)
table(sub$Leiden <- factor(. <- k$membership, labels=letters[seq_along(unique(.))]))
```
#### Seurat object

The same as before can be done with `Seurat` but some changes in the code would be needed:
The  applied in the quality control code applied by default the Louvain algorithm to iteratively group cells together. However, Leiden is generally considered the **current best-practice choice for graph/community detection clustering** in scRNA-seq because it fixes known issues of Louvain (most famously: Louvain can produce disconnected communities), and tends to be more stable/robust. Many best-practice guides explicitly recommend Leiden over Louvain nowadays.

In Seurat, Leiden is algorithm = 4 in FindClusters() (after building the neighbor graph):
```{r}
pvp$louvain_clusters <- pvp$seurat_cluster.sketched # Saving the QC clustering
# Leiden clustering
pvp <- FindClusters(pvp, cluster.name = "seurat_cluster.sketched", graph.name = "sketch_nn", algorithm = 4, resolution = 2.6)
pvp$leiden_clusters <- pvp$seurat_cluster.sketched
DimPlot(pvp, group.by = "louvain_clusters", label = TRUE)
DimPlot(pvp, group.by = "leiden_clusters", label = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Saving pvp data
saveRDS(pvp, file = paste0(path,"/RDS/",fl,".rds"))
log_msg("RDS file saved.")
```

If it is a `Seurat` object the unsupervised algorithms will be **based on the Principal Components** extracted from performing the PCA. **But after getting the clusters (with `FindClusters()` function) it is advised to find markers (genes) that define clusters via differential expression (DE)**. Seurat by default, it identifies positive and negative markers of a single cluster (specified in ident.1), compared to all other cells. `FindAllMarkers()` automates this process for all clusters, but you can also test groups of clusters vs. each other, or against all cells.
```{r echo=FALSE}
# find all markers of cluster 2
cluster2.markers <- FindMarkers(pvp, ident.1 = 2)
head(cluster2.markers, n = 5)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# find all markers distinguishing cluster 5 from clusters 0 and 3
cluster5.markers <- FindMarkers(pvp, ident.1 = 5, ident.2 = c(0, 3))
head(cluster5.markers, n = 5)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
###############################################################################
#        If the RDS was not saved
###############################################################################
# find markers for every cluster compared to all remaining cells, report only the positive
# ones
pvp.markers <- FindAllMarkers(pvp, only.pos = TRUE)
# Saving the results in the Seurat object and then saving it locally
pvp@misc$markers <- pvp.markers
# Saving pvp data
saveRDS(pvp, file = paste0(path,"/RDS/",fl,".rds"))
log_msg("RDS file saved.")

###############################################################################
#        If the RDS was saved
# IMPORTANT: FIND ALL MARKERS WAS MADE USING LOUVAIN ALGORITHM
###############################################################################
#pvp <- readRDS(paste0(path,"/RDS/",fl,".rds")) # In Rmd this line has to be executed in the terminal
#pvp.markers = pvp@misc$markers

pvp.markers %>%
    group_by(cluster) %>%
    dplyr::filter(abs(avg_log2FC) > 1)
```

`DoHeatmap()` generates an expression heatmap for given cells and features. In this case, we are plotting the top 10 markers (or all markers if less than 10) for each cluster.

```{r}
# To solve the error non-unique values when setting 'row.names' 
# The error was due to NaNs cause by it not locking at the sketched data (the one that was clusterized)
# When looking at the results of the clustering the full data didn't have clusters assigns to all the entries
DefaultAssay(pvp) <- "sketch" 

top5 <- pvp@misc$markers %>% 
  group_by(cluster) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(abs(avg_log2FC) > 1) %>% 
  slice_max(order_by = abs(avg_log2FC), n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%

genes <- unique(top5$gene)

p <- DotPlot(object = pvp, features = genes,group.by = "leiden_clusters") + 
  RotatedAxis() + 
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8, angle = 90, hjust = 1),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8)
  )

ggsave(filename = paste0(path,"/dotplot_wide.png"), plot = p, width = 30, height = 12, dpi = 300)
```
If the plots show that some genes are highly expressed for unique cell types we can check and use them for a supervised analysis after.

The used filters (not extracted from anywhere, just us being restrictive so we can work faster):
abs(avg_log2FC) > 0.25
Keeps genes with fairly strong upregulation in that cluster. Since log2FC of 1 means about a 2-fold difference, this is a fairly strict effect-size cutoff. In single-cell RNA-seq (e.g., Seurat), a lower threshold of 0.25 is commonly used, while intermediate studies often use 0.58 ($\approx$1.5-fold change).

p_val_adj < 0.05
Keeps genes that are statistically significant after multiple-testing correction.

pct.1 > 0.2
Keeps genes expressed in at least 20% of cells in that cluster, which helps remove genes that look significant only because of a tiny number of cells.

```{r, out.width="70%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Annotations/DU53/dotplot_wide.png")
``` 

```{r}
marker_table_summary <- pvp@misc$markers %>%
  dplyr::filter(abs(avg_log2FC) > 0.25, p_val_adj < 0.05, pct.1 > 0.2) %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(avg_log2FC)), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(
    top_markers = paste(head(gene, 10), collapse = ", "),
    n_markers = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

marker_table_summary
```

Depending on the case of the dataset, we can use canonical markers to easily match the unbiased clustering to known cell types. What we are going to do here is use **PanglaoDB** to get a preliminary cell type per cluster, then we are going to make confirm or change our preliminary cell type with the **Go terms** of each top 5 gene per cluster and finally we are going to confirm it with **Gene Cards** by checking if the genes are related with the cellular function of the suspected cell type.

However if we still are not sure about one cellular type there's still the supervised method's result we are going to compare to these ones.

**With PanglaoDB:**

Let's make use of the `getMarkers()` function of rPanglaoDB (https://github.com/dosorio/rPanglaoDB)
   
```{r}
#install.packages("rPanglaoDB")
library(rPanglaoDB)

# Example input:
# df_top10 has columns: cluster, gene
# one row per gene, 10 genes per cluster

get_top3_from_getMarkers <- function(genes, cluster) {
    res <- tryCatch({
    rPanglaoDB::getMarkers(include = genes) %>%
    dplyr::filter(Specie == "Homo sapiens")
  }, error = function(e) {
    message("getMarkers failed for: ", paste("Cluster: ", cluster, "\n Genes: " ,genes, collapse = ", "))
    return(NULL)
  })

  if (is.null(res) || nrow(res) == 0) {
    return(data.frame(cell_type = NA_character_, n_hits = 0))
  }
  res %>%
    count(`Cell-Type`, sort = TRUE) %>%
    slice_head(n = 3) %>%
    rename(cell_type = `Cell-Type`, n_hits = n)
}

top3_list <- marker_table_summary %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  group_split() %>%
  lapply(function(x) {
    genes <- head(unlist(strsplit(x$top_markers[1], ",\\s*")), 4)
    out <- get_top3_from_getMarkers(genes, x$cluster)
    out$cluster <- unique(x$cluster)
    out
  })

top3_results <- bind_rows(top3_list) %>%
  select(cluster, everything())

top3_results
```

## Supervised

Despite having said before that supervised methods can not be used in this data due to the lack of reference, using SingleR is correct here as they use pure cell types trasncriptomes. It is no going to be as accurate in cell type prediction as it would be with a reference but be can be certain that is going to be unbiased.    

#### Spatial Experiment object
First, the `Spatial Experiment` object algorithms.

For comparison, we annotate the Xenium data using a label transfer approach, `SingleR`, which relies on labeled scRNA-seq data to compute references profiles and transfers labels based on the rank correlation between observed (here, Xenium) and reference (scRNA-seq) expression profiles.

First, we retrieve a matching (Chromium) scRNA-seq dataset, which includes low- (Level1) and high-resolution (Level2) annotations of cells into 9 and 31 subpopulations, respectively. This is the whole loading and preprocessing of the reference dataset in the Spatial Experiment object annotation tutorial (third link in the end) :

```r
# retrieve dataset from OSF repository
id <- "Chromium_HumanColon_Oliveira"
pa <- OSTA.data_load(id)
dir.create(td <- tempfile())
unzip(pa, exdir=td)
# read into 'SingleCellExperiment'
sce <- read10xCounts(list.files(td, "h5$", full.names=TRUE))
cd <- read.csv(list.files(td, "cell_meta", full.names=TRUE))
colData(sce) <- cbind(colData(sce), cd[, -1])
table(sce$Level1) # tabulate low-res. labels
ncol(sce) # overall number of cells
# exclude cells deemed to be of low-quality
sce <- sce[, sce$QCFilter == "Keep"]
# subset cells from same patient
sce <- sce[, grepl("P2", sce$Patient)]
# realize count matrix
assay(sce) <- as(assay(sce), "dgCMatrix")
# log-library size normalization
sce <- logNormCounts(sce)
# restrict to Xenium targets
sce <- sce[rowData(sce)$ID %in% rowData(sub)$ID, ]
# set gene symbols as feature names
rownames(sce) <- rowData(sce)$Symbol
```

The dataset used in the DUTRENEO paper was “BlueprintEncodeData” reference dataset which included a number of different cell types. To minimize false positive assignments, we restricted the “main labels” of the reference to cell types that may populate bladder tumours: epithelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle, pericytes, neurons, monocytes, CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, NK cells, B cells, macrophages, endothelial cells, dendritic cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils. 
```{r echo = FALSE}
# 1. Load the reference dataset

ref.data.bpe <- BlueprintEncodeData(ensembl=FALSE) # Params indicate to use gene symbols (when set to FALSE instead of 19859 TSPAN6 we have ENSG00000000003 and only 6)
print(ref.data.bpe)
# Keep only selected main labels
keep <- ref.data.bpe$label.main %in% c("Epithelial cells","Fibroblasts",
                                       "Smooth muscle", "Pericytes","Neurons",
                                       "Monocytes", "CD4+ T-cells","CD8+ T-cells",
                                       "B-cells", "NK cells", "Macrophages",
                                       "Endothelial cells", "Neutrophils",
                                       "Eosinophils", "DC")
ref.sub <- ref.data.bpe[, keep]
print(unique(ref.sub$label.main))
# 2. Extract expression data (normalized data is usually in the "data" slot)
test_data <- GetAssayData(pvp, assay = "Xenium", layer = "data")
head(test_data)
```

Here, we run **SingleR** using Level2 (high-resolution) annotations and with argument aggr.ref=TRUE, such that reference profiles will be aggregated (per cluster) prior to annotation. In this way, every Xenium cell will be assigned a label based on which pseudo-bulk scRNA-seq profile represents the best match.

```{r}
# set parallelization
bp <- MulticoreParam(4)

# perform label transfer at the single cell-level,
# using pseudo-bulk Chromium profiles as reference
res <- SingleR(
    test=test_data, ref=ref.sub, 
    labels=ref.sub$label.fine, 
    aggr.ref=TRUE, BPPARAM=bp)
print(length(unique(ref.sub$label.main)))

# Saving the results in the Seurat object and then saving it locally
pvp@misc$singleR <- res
# Saving pvp data
saveRDS(pvp, file = paste0(path,"/RDS/",fl,".rds"))
log_msg("RDS file saved.")

tab_labels <- sort(table(pvp@misc$singleR$labels), decreasing = TRUE) 
tab_labels # We have 43 unique labels inside the 259 fine labels of the reference
```

```r
plotScoreHeatmap(res) # Takes too long in my computer
```
We identify poor-quality or ambiguous assignments based on the per-cell “delta”, i.e., the difference between the score for the assigned label and the median across all labels for each cell. Our assumption is that most of the labels in the reference are not relevant to any given cell. Thus, the median across all labels can be used as a measure of the baseline correlation, while the gap from the assigned label to this baseline can be used as a measure of the assignment confidence.

Low deltas indicate that the assignment is uncertain, possibly because the cell’s true label does not exist in the reference. An obvious next step is to apply a threshold on the delta to filter out these low-confidence assignments. We use the delta rather than the assignment score as the latter is more sensitive to technical effects. For example, changes in library size affect the technical noise and can increase/decrease all scores for a given cell, while the delta is somewhat more robust as it focuses on the differences between scores within each cell. 

The `pruneScores()` function in the R package SingleR is used to remove low-quality or ambiguous cell type assignments in single-cell RNA-seq data. The example below discards cells with deltas below an arbitrary threshold of 0.2, where higher thresholds correspond to greater assignment certainty.

Cells that had a low confidence score by SingleR were labeled "unassigned" in the DUTRENEO papaer instead of removed.
```{r}
pvp$singler_labels <- res$labels
p1 <- ImageDimPlot(
  object = pvp,
  fov = "fov",
  boundaries = "centroids",
  group.by = "singler_labels",
  cols = "polychrome",
  axes = TRUE
) 
ggsave(filename = paste0(path,"/DU53_clusters_FROMrawSingleR.png"), plot = p1, width = 12, height = 12, dpi = 300)

res <- pvp@misc$singleR
# min.diff.med	= Numeric scalar specifying the minimum acceptable delta for each cell.
# low_confi <- pruneScores(res, min.diff.med = 0.3)  # N Unassigned = 400237 
# low_confi <- pruneScores(res, min.diff.med = 0.2) # N Unassigned = 228268
low_confi <- pruneScores(res, min.diff.med = 0.1)  # N Unassigned = 50775
res$labels[low_confi] <- "Unassigned"
tab_labels <- sort(table(res$labels), decreasing = TRUE) 
tab_labels
```

According to the DUTRENEO paper, the final list of cell types which we could confidently represent in our Xenium samples are: epithelial cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle, neurons, granulocytes, monocytes, CD4 T cells, Tregs, CD8 T cells, NK cells, B cells, plasma cells, macrophages, macrophages M1, macrophages M2, and DCs. Cells that had a low confidence score by SingleR were labeled “unassigned”.

## Confirming SingleR annotations

`clustree()` function to get at which resolution should the clustering be made when no annotating data is present. We can use its results to see if the labels chosen in SingleR are good (explanation below). (**IMPORTANT: SingleR is designed to handle batch effects between the reference dataset (used for training) and the test dataset (single-cell data being annotated)**)
```{r}

resolutions <- c(0.1,0.5, 0.8,1,1.5,2,2.5,3,3.5,4,4.5,5)
for (res in resolutions){
  DefaultAssay(pvp) <- "sketch"
  pvp <- FindClusters(object = pvp,cluster.name = paste0("sketchedRES.",res), resolution = res, algorithm = 4)
}
# Saving pvp data
saveRDS(pvp, file = paste0(path,"/RDS/",fl,".rds"))
log_msg("RDS file saved.")
```

```{r}
# Plot the tree
#DefaultAssay(pvp) <- "sketch" # Clustree don't use the usbset but the metada object so NaNs will afect its process
# To avoid NaNs problems
cols <- grep("^sketchedRES\\.", colnames(pvp@meta.data), value = TRUE)
keep <- complete.cases(pvp@meta.data[, cols, drop = FALSE])
pvp_clean <- subset(pvp, cells = rownames(pvp@meta.data)[keep])

p <- clustree::clustree(pvp_clean, prefix = "sketchedRES.")
ggsave(filename = paste0(path,"/Clustree_", fl,".png"), plot = p, width = 12, height = 20)
p
```
The cluster trees must be understood like the connexion between whole clusters of diferent resolutions and how each data point passes from one cluster to the other:
- Higher resolution → more clusters
- Each row = one resolution
- Each circle = one cluster
- Arrows = how cells move between clusters when resolution increases
- The color of the edge = number of cells transferred
- If the arrows are:
  - purple → few cells
  - yellow → many cells

So, why is this usefull for our cell clustering ? Well that's because if the cluster persists across resolutions it means it is biologically meaningful. When the arrows go straight from the parent node and stays teh same or divides into 2 it means its being more precise about one cell type, maybe differentiating the function they are perfoming at that moment. 

If those exact same arrows have a soft color that mean that the percentage of cells that when to one cluster to another is very minimal that given how complex is biology it makes sense but just while the amount of cells is small. Once the arrows have stronger colors they menaing is not biologically meaning full but more caotic ore overclustered.

Let's look at the gene expression of each cluster to be able extract more conclusions about the goodness of these clusters. 

The following code was extracted from [this paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6057528)
```{r seurat-genes, fig.cap = "Clustering trees of the PBMC dataset coloured according to the expression of known markers. The node colours indicate the average of the log~2~ gene counts of samples in each cluster. CD19 (A) identifies B cells, CD14 (B) shows a population of monocytes, CD3D (C) is a marker of T cells and CCR7 (D) shows the split between memory and naive CD4 T cells."}

plots <- lapply(c("CD19", "CD14", "CD3D", "CCR7"), function(x) {
    clustree(pvp_clean, node_colour = x, node_colour_aggr = "mean",
             node_size_range = c(3, 10), node_text_size = 2,
             edge_width = 1.2, prefix = "sketchedRES.") +
    scale_colour_viridis(option = "plasma", begin = 0.3) +
    guides(size = FALSE,
           colour = guide_colourbar(title = x,
                                    barwidth = unit(3, "mm"),
                                    barheight = unit(35, "mm"),
                                    order = 1),
           edge_colour = FALSE,
           edge_alpha = FALSE) +
    theme(legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 9))
})

legend <- get_legend(plots[[1]] +
                         guides(size = guide_legend(title = "Cluster size",
                                                    title.position = "top",
                                                    title.hjust = 0.5,
                                                    label.position = "top",
                                                    label.hjust = 0.5,
                                                    order = 1),
                                colour = FALSE,
                                edge_colour = guide_edge_colourbar(
                                    title = "Sample count",
                                    title.position = "top",
                                    title.hjust = 0.5,
                                    barwidth = 12,
                                    draw.ulim = TRUE,
                                    draw.llim = TRUE,
                                    order = 3),
                                edge_alpha = guide_legend(
                                    title = "In-proportion",
                                    title.position = "top",
                                    title.hjust = 0.5,
                                    label.position = "top",
                                    label.hjust = 0.5,
                                    keywidth = 4,
                                    order = 4)) +
                         theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
panel <- plot_grid(plotlist = plots,
                   labels = c("A - CD19", "B - CD14", "C - CD3D", "D - CCR7"),
                   label_size = 20, ncol =2)

ggsave(filename = paste0(path,"/clustree_seurat_genes.png"), 
       plot = panel, width = 16, height = 12, dpi = 300)

include_graphics(paste0(path,"/clustree_seurat_genes.png"))
```

It seems like the best precision is 4, 5 and 6. At these levels, most clusters are derived directly from their parent nodes, which results in very few diagonal edges in the clustree plot. Additionally, none of these edges are strongly colored, indicating that only a small percentage of cells change cluster assignments drastically between these resolutions. We will select the fifth one as it is the middle of the accepted ones, which corresponds to the one with .


Another way of checking the SingleR results is to plot the labels in the tissue itself. Here finally the biological complexity will help us out as the labels MUST present some kind of structure in other to confirm that they are correct and biologically meaningful.

Looking at the overall image we can clearly see some structure, with cluster cells having limits made out of other cell types. The mix of cells types in the surrounding clusters is normal and part of the biological complexity of tissues. Another good indicator is that the big soft red (pinkish) cluster is made out of epithelial cells !!! Which is the most common type of cell in bladder cancer !!!

Another important thing to mention is that unassigned cells (bright green) seem to mostly group themselves arround the epithelial and B-cells clusters.


<span style="background-color: yellow">The ovelarp between the choosen cluster and the SingleR results is a very good indicator that the choosen labels are correct. The idea would be to plot the SingleR labels in the chosen cluster's UMAP and see the distribution of each label.</span>

Plot the distribution as a bar plot:

From this clustering we can conclude that the epithelial cells are well defined in two separated clusters (maybe one tumoral and the other healthy epithelial cells, we will find out later). Also a big percentage of the clusters have a main label that can be assigned to with confidence. However, there are still some clusters that do not have a main dominant label but they were rather clustered together by other thing that were NOT cell type. So these clusters are good but they still need some help to identify all the remaining cell types.

Now, we will extract the clusters we consider to have a secure label (relative abundance above thershold per majority class in the cluster).
```{r}
# count cells per leiden cluster x singler label
df <- pvp@meta.data %>%
  dplyr::count(sketchedRES.1.5, singler_labels, name = "n") %>%
  group_by(sketchedRES.1.5) %>%
  mutate(freq = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

# dominant label per cluster
dominant_clusters <- df %>%
  group_by(sketchedRES.1.5) %>%
  slice_max(freq, n = 2, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(desc(freq))

print(dominant_clusters)

# Sketching out the clusters we now for sure have a label
threshold <- 0.75   # 75%

# Above 0.75% for one label or for one label + unassigned label
unconcrete_clusters <- dominant_clusters %>%
  group_by(sketchedRES.1.5) %>%
  # Filter OUT clusters that meet your "confident" criteria
  dplyr::filter(!any(
    # Condition 1: Single label > 75%
    freq > threshold | 
    # Condition 2: Top label + Unassigned > 75%
    (sum(freq[singler_labels %in% c(singler_labels[1], "Unassigned")]) > threshold)
  )) %>%
  pull(sketchedRES.1.5) %>%
  as.character() %>%
  unique() %>%
  stats::na.omit()
print(unconcrete_clusters)

# make sure the active identities are the clustering you want to use
Idents(pvp) <- "sketchedRES.1.5"

# keep only the unconcrete clusters
pvp_unconcrete <- subset(pvp, idents = unconcrete_clusters)

pvp_unconcrete
```

But this process requires too much human on the loop and we must do this for all the samples we have, so let's automate it !
`AggregateExpression()` simply sums all the counts of that gene in the space, in biology it is better to use the average as agrupations of genes in the sample might bias the calculations (lot's of genes because it is highly expressed in one section not because there are lot's of that cell type in the cluster). Let's try it with `AverageExpression` or `AddModuleScore`
```{r}

# 1. Get average expression for your specific marker genes
# We use the 'RNA' assay (or 'SCT') and the specific gene list you defined
avg_singler <- AverageExpression(pvp_unconcrete, 
                                 group.by = "singler_labels", 
                                 features = genes_v2)$SCT

avg_leiden <- AverageExpression(pvp_unconcrete, # Average o AddModule Score
                                group.by = "sketchedRES.1.5", 
                                features = genes_v2)$SCT

# 2. Calculate Spearman correlation between the two matrices
cor_matrix <- cor(as.matrix(avg_leiden), as.matrix(avg_singler), method = "spearman")

# 3. Visualize
pheatmap(cor_matrix, 
         main = "Correlation: Leiden Clusters vs SingleR Labels",
         color = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(100),
         display_numbers = TRUE, # Shows the correlation value in the box
         angle_col = 45)
```

Marc, my supervisor, already tried using different algorithms but there was no better outcome. So instead of using other algorithms let's try using a **reduced cell type list** can help *SingelR* to achieve better results.


## Small break to check if fewer labels improve the annotation process
Changes we are going to make in the annotation list are:
- We are going to group CD4, CD8 and Tregs under B-cells.
- Macrophages M1 and M2 grouped under Macrophages
- Neurons label is going to be removed
- Plasma cells has the posisbility of being grouped under B-cells in the future but let's leave just for now.

```{r}
ref.data.bpe <- BlueprintEncodeData(ensembl=FALSE) 
print(ref.data.bpe)
# Keep only selected main labels
keep <- ref.data.bpe$label.main %in% c("Epithelial cells","Fibroblasts",
                                       "Smooth muscle", "Pericytes",
                                       "Monocytes", "CD4+ T-cells","CD8+ T-cells",
                                       "B-cells", "NK cells", "Macrophages",
                                       "Endothelial cells", "Neutrophils",
                                       "Eosinophils", "DC")
ref.sub <- ref.data.bpe[, keep]
print(unique(ref.sub$label.main))
# Extract expression data (normalized data is usually in the "data" slot)
test_data <- GetAssayData(pvp, assay = "Xenium", layer = "data")
head(test_data)
```

```{r} 
ref.sub$label.fine[ref.sub$label.fine == "Pericytes"] <- "Smooth muscle"
ref.sub$label.fine[ref.sub$label.fine == "mv Endothelial cells"] <- "Endothelial cells"
ref.sub$label.fine[ref.sub$label.fine %in% c("CD4+ Tcm", "CD4+ Tem", "CD8+ Tcm", "CD8+ Tem", "Tregs", "CD4+ T-cells", "CD8+ T-cells")] <- "T-cells"
ref.sub$label.fine[ref.sub$label.fine %in% c("Neutrophils", "Eosinophils")] <- "Granulocytes"
ref.sub$label.fine[ref.sub$label.fine %in% c("Macrophages M1", "Macrophages M2")] <- "Macrophages"
ref.sub$label.fine[ref.sub$label.fine %in% c("naive B-cells", "Class-switched memory B-cells", "Memory B-cells")] <- "B-cells"

print(unique(ref.sub$label.fine))
```
Now this is the reduced list we want to work with to see if the algorithm can work better !
```{r}

```{r}
# count cells per cluster x SingleR label
df <- pvp@meta.data %>%
  dplyr::count(ReducedRES.1, singler_labels, name = "n") %>%
  group_by(ReducedRES.1) %>%
  mutate(freq = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

# top labels per cluster
dominant_clusters <- df %>%
  group_by(ReducedRES.1) %>%
  slice_max(freq, n = 2, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(ReducedRES.1, desc(freq))

threshold <- 0.75

# initialize final labels in original object
pvp$Final_Labels <- "Unconcrete"

# clusters confidently labeled by SingleR
# Above 0.75% for one label or for one label + unassigned label
concrete_clusters <- dominant_clusters %>%
  group_by(ReducedRES.1) %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    # Condition 1: Single label > 75%
    any(freq > threshold) |
    # Condition 2: Top label + Unassigned > 75%
    any(sum(freq[singler_labels %in% c(singler_labels[1], "Unassigned")]) > threshold)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() 

# assign the top non-Unassigned label to those confident clusters
cluster_labels <- concrete_clusters %>%
  #dplyr::filter(singler_labels != "Unassigned") %>%
  group_by(ReducedRES.1) %>%
  slice_max(freq, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::select(ReducedRES.1, assigned_label = singler_labels)

for(i in seq_len(nrow(cluster_labels))) {
  cl <- cluster_labels$ReducedRES.1[i]
  lab <- cluster_labels$assigned_label[i]
  cells_use <- rownames(pvp@meta.data)[pvp$ReducedRES.1 == cl]
  pvp$Final_Labels[cells_use] <- lab
}

table(pvp$Final_Labels[pvp$ReducedRES.1 == "2"])

# subset only ambiguous clusters

## Continue with the refinement with the markers

The `DotPlot()` genes per each cell type show that epithelial cells have very unique gene sigsnatures compared to the other cell type in the SingleR annotations. So first, we can assign with confidence the Epithelial label to the cell that SingleR considered Epithelial. 


Here we will take profit of `AddModuleScore()` function and the FindAllmarkers result. The first one can help us compare the log2 fold cahnge between two cell types that are very similar and the second one helps us when they are 3. So, how should it be understood ?
<span style="background-color: yellow">
`AddModuleScore` calculates the average expression levels of each program (cluster) on single cell level, subtracted by the aggregated expression of control gene sets (background). All analyzed genes are binned based on averaged expression, and the control genes are randomly selected from each bin.
So, when we do res = log2(T-cells/NK cells), being T-cells and NK cells the results for each from `AddModuleScore`, we can have 3 situations:
- res >= 1 ==> implies that T-cells
- res < 0 ==> implies that NK
- -1 < res < 1 ==> Unnassigned

In contrast, using this ratio with `AddModuleScore` is problematic because:
- Scores can be negative, making the ratio undefined or meaningless
- Scores can be zero, leading to division errors or infinite values
- The scores are already background-corrected differences, so applying a ratio distorts their interpretation

Therefore, while `AddModuleScore` is useful for detecting expression above background, `AddModuleScore_UCell` is better suited for direct comparison between gene programs using ratios, as in our case. Its rank-based, positive, and bounded scores provide a more stable and interpretable framework for distinguishing between T-cell and NK-cell signatures.
</span>

THIS FUNCTION IS NOT QUITE USEFUL AS THE LOG 2 FOLD CHANGE SHOULD BE MADE WITH THE RESULTS FROM FINDALLMARKERS THAT ALREADY GIVES YOU THE LOGARITHM.
```{r}
compute_pairwise_scores_singleR <- function(
  seurat_obj, scores, celltype_1, celltype_2, singleR_col = "singler_labels", eps = 1e-6, update_seurat = FALSE) {
  
  # Obtain SingleR labels
  singleR_labels <- seurat_obj@meta.data[rownames(scores), singleR_col, drop = TRUE]
  
  # To keep only cells previously assigned by SingleR to one of the two types
  cells_keep <- rownames(scores)[singleR_labels %in% c(celltype_1, celltype_2)]
  
  if (length(cells_keep) == 0) {
    stop("No cells found with SingleR labels matching the requested cell types")
  }
  if(celltype_1 == "T-cells"){celltype_1= "CD4+ T-cells"}
  else if(celltype_2 == "T-cells"){celltype_2= "CD4+ T-cells"}
  
  m <- as.matrix(scores[cells_keep, c(celltype_1, celltype_2), drop = FALSE])
  
  score_1 <- m[, celltype_1]
  score_2 <- m[, celltype_2]
  
  log2ratio <- log2((score_1 + eps) / (score_2 + eps))
  label <- ifelse(
    log2ratio >= 1, celltype_1,
    ifelse(log2ratio <= -1, celltype_2, "Unassigned")
  )
  
  res <- data.frame(
    SingleR_label = seurat_obj@meta.data[cells_keep, singleR_col, drop = TRUE],
    score_1 = score_1,
    score_2 = score_2,
    log2ratio = log2ratio,
    label = label,
    row.names = rownames(m)
  )
  cat("\n=== Computed labels ===\n")
  lab_tab <- table(res$label, useNA = "ifany")
  print(lab_tab[order(names(lab_tab))])
  
  cat("\n=== SingleR labels ===\n")
  sr_tab <- table(res$SingleR_label, useNA = "ifany")
  print(sr_tab[order(names(sr_tab))])
  
  if (update_seurat){
     # Cells to update (exclude Unassigned)
    cells_update <- rownames(res)[res$label != "Unassigned"]
    
    cat("\n=== Updating Seurat metadata ===\n")
    cat("Cells updated:", length(cells_update), "\n")
    
    # Perform update safely
    seurat_obj$Final_Labels[cells_update] <- res[cells_update, "label"]
    
    return(list(res = res, seurat_obj = seurat_obj))
  }
  
  else { return(res) }
}
```

Final_Labels was created for these specified labels and we do not have to worry about modifying other concreted labels as the scores were selected only for the unconcrete clusters. We could add a variable in the function above to assign the chosen labels to Final_Labels.

Now we can use `FindAllMarkers` function to the rest of our analysis. IMPORTANT! The code where the concrete_clusters were assigned is necessary to run the following chunks of code.

```{r}
# 1. Use those labels as identities
Idents(pvp) <- "singler_labels" # So that the clusters in FindAllMarkers are the cell types

# 2. Use RNA assay for marker finding
DefaultAssay(pvp) <- "SCT"

markers <- FindAllMarkers(
  pvp,
  only.pos = TRUE,
  min.pct = 0.25,
  logfc.threshold = 0.25
)

# 3. Top 10 genes per cell type
# Keep only statistically significant positive markers
# - p_val_adj < 0.05: significant after multiple-testing correction
# - abs(avg_log2FC) > 0: gene is more expressed in that cell type than in the others
markers_sig <- markers %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    p_val_adj < 0.05, # p_val corrected for multiple testing (e.g. Bonferroni)
    abs(avg_log2FC) > 0
)

# For each cell type, keep the top 10 genes with the highest positive log fold-change
top10_genesXcellType <- markers_sig %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = abs(avg_log2FC), n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

# Inspect result
top10_genesXcellType

This code reshapes the Seurat metadata to keep only cells where the assigned label (`celltype`, from SingleR) matches the corresponding signature score (e.g., B-cell score in B-cells), then removes missing values. It then performs an ANOVA followed by a Tukey HSD post-hoc test to compare mean scores across cell types. Finally, it checks whether **all pairwise differences between cell types are statistically significant** (adjusted p-value < 0.05).

```{r}
score_df <- pvp@meta.data %>%
  mutate(celltype = singler_labels) %>%
  dplyr::select(celltype, starts_with("Score_")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-celltype, names_to = "signature", values_to = "score") %>%
  mutate(signature = sub("^Score_", "", signature)) %>%
  dplyr::filter(celltype == signature, !is.na(score))

tukey_df <- TukeyHSD(aov(score ~ celltype, data = score_df))$celltype %>%
  as.data.frame()

# This returns:
# TRUE → all cell types are significantly different from each other
# FALSE → at least one pair is not significantly different
print(all(tukey_df$`p adj` < 0.05))
```
```{r}
# To see which pairs are not different:
tukey_df[tukey_df$`p adj` >= 0.05, ]
```

After comparing the average expression of the most expressed genes per cell type across all the labeled cell by SingleR we can see that the cells annotated as **NK cells, Granulocytes, Monocytes and DC cells** are not confident enough. The next step here is to do the whole process again but with only this subset.

```{r}
# Getting which cell types are unconcrete
mismatched_cell_types <- names(signatures)[
  sapply(names(signatures), function(ct) {
    idx <- which(as.character(plot_df$signature) == ct)
    if (length(idx) == 0) return(TRUE)
    sub <- plot_df[idx, ]
    best_label <- as.character(sub$singler_label)[which.max(sub$sum_score)]
    best_label != ct
  })
]

mismatched_cell_types
```
```{r}
# Making subset of ONLY unconcrete cell types
pvp_subset <- subset(
  pvp,
  subset = singler_labels %in% setdiff(mismatched_cell_types, "Unassigned")
)
```

```{r}
# 1. Use those labels as identities
Idents(pvp_subset) <- "singler_labels" # So that the clusters in FindAllMarkers are the cell types

# 2. Use RNA assay for marker finding
DefaultAssay(pvp_subset) <- "SCT"

markers_subset <- FindAllMarkers(
  pvp_subset, only.pos = TRUE, min.pct = 0.25, logfc.threshold = 0.25)

# 3. Top 10 genes per cell type
# Keep only statistically significant positive markers
# - p_val_adj < 0.05: significant after multiple-testing correction
# - abs(avg_log2FC) > 0: gene is more expressed in that cell type than in the others
markers_sig <- markers_subset %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    p_val_adj < 0.05, # p_val corrected for multiple tetsing (e.g. Bonferroni)
    abs(avg_log2FC) > 0
)

# For each cell type, keep the top 10 genes with the highest positive log fold-change
SUBSET_top10_genesXcellType <- markers_sig %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = abs(avg_log2FC), n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

# Inspect result
SUBSET_top10_genesXcellType
```


```{r}

celltypes <- names(signatures_subset)
colnames(pvp_subset@meta.data)[match(score_cols, colnames(pvp_subset@meta.data))] <- paste0("Score_", celltypes)

  ) %>%

# NK cells

  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "SingleR label",
    y = "Sum of AddModuleScore",
    title = "NK cells signature score across SingleR labels"
)

We should check if the DC cells are different from the monocytes as their sum of AddModuleScore is pretty close. Also we should make it for the granulocytes and monocytes as the first ones seem to be cells with low expression. --> How can we know this automatically ? Q la label del titulo sea la maxima en el plot y que la segunda no esté muy cerca de la primera

```{r}
# Getting which cell types are not differentiable
# - The best label in the plot coincides with the title
# - The second best label is not really close to the first one.
mismatched_cell_types <- lapply(names(signatures_subset), function(ct) {
  sub <- plot_df %>%
    dplyr::filter(signature == ct) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sum_score))
  
  best_lab <- as.character(sub$singler_label[1])
  second_lab <- as.character(sub$singler_label[2])
  best_score <- sub$sum_score[1]
  second_score <- sub$sum_score[2]
  
  labs <- c(
    # Condition 1: best label must match the signature/title
    if (best_lab != ct) c(ct, best_lab),
    # Condition 2: second best must not be too close to the first one
    if ((best_score - second_score) / abs(best_score) <= 0.1) c(best_lab, second_lab)
  )
  
  if (length(labs)) setNames(list(unique(labs)), ct) else NULL
})

mismatched_cell_types <- mismatched_cell_types[!sapply(mismatched_cell_types, is.null)]
mismatched_cell_types
```



Here we shouldn't do our function compute_pairwise... we should do FindMarkers (*it already gives the log2fold, no need to compute it*) between each group we are unsure about !!!!
```{r}
# Function to print pretty the markers per cell type
pretty_print_markers <- function(markers_list) {
  for (name in names(markers_list)) {
    cat("\n", paste0("=== ", name, " ==="), "\n")
    cat(paste(markers_list[[name]], collapse = ", "), "\n")
  }
}
# Code 
Idents(pvp_subset) <- "singler_labels" 
DefaultAssay(pvp_subset) <- "SCT"

DC.vs.Monocytes <- FindMarkers(pvp_subset, ident.1 = "DC", ident.2="Monocytes", logfc.threshold = 0.25)
head(DC.vs.Monocytes, n = 10)

# take top positive genes for each side as signatures
markers_DC <- DC.vs.Monocytes %>%
  dplyr::filter(avg_log2FC > 0.5, p_val_adj < 0.05) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(avg_log2FC)) %>%
  head(20) %>%
  rownames()

markers_mono <- DC.vs.Monocytes %>%
  dplyr::filter(avg_log2FC < -0.5, p_val_adj < 0.05) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(avg_log2FC) %>%
  head(20) %>%
  rownames()

signatures <- list(
  DC = markers_DC,
  Monocytes = markers_mono
)

pvp_subset <- AddModuleScore_UCell(pvp_subset, features = signatures, name = NULL)

pretty_print_markers(signatures)
VlnPlot(pvp_subset, features = c("DC", "Monocytes"), group.by = "singler_labels", pt.size = 0)
```

Cells significantly expressed in T-cells para distinguir cd4, cd8 y tregs --> Two ways:
- o seurat clustering with different resolutions o k-mean clustering (aiming to 3 clusters) and then look to the markers ==> All bad
- o using SingleR with these 3 labels from the beggining

The second approach might change the classification results, as it would be interesting to know investigate the differences we will to the first aproach in this markdown here and then the second one on the *Final_Annotation_Xenium*.

To the clustering we could use the `FindClusters`and `Clustree` functions to know at which resolution we can have 3 clusters, but as a very low resolution would be needed for sure and to investigate new things we will use k-means algorithm !

`GetAssayData(pbmc_small)` returns a matrix of genes × cells:
- rows = genes
- columns = cells

`Embeddings(tcells, "pca")` returns a matrix with:
- rows = cells
- columns = PCA dimensions

Useful canonical markers:
- CD4 T cells: IL7R, LTB, MALAT1, LTB, MHC class II low, often CCR7, LTB
- CD8 T cells: CD8A, CD8B, NKG7, CCL5, GZMK, GZMB, PRF1
- Tregs: FOXP3, IL2RA, TIGIT, CTLA4, IKZF2, LAYN

```{r}
# Clustree
resolutions <- c(0.02,0.04,0.05,0.06,0.08,0.09,0.1,0.2)
DefaultAssay(tcells) <- "SCT"
for (res in resolutions){
  tcells <- FindClusters(object = tcells,graph.name = "sketch_snn",cluster.name = paste0("ReducedRES.",res), resolution = res, algorithm = 4)
}

# To avoid NaNs problems
# cells that are actually in the sketch graph
sketch_cells <- rownames(tcells@graphs$sketch_snn)
# subset object to those cells only
tcells_sketch <- subset(tcells, cells = sketch_cells)

# now metadata columns ReducedRES.* should have no NAs
p <- clustree::clustree(tcells_sketch@meta.data, prefix = "ReducedRES.")
p
```
